procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed criminal revision petitions in the Madras High Court against the orders of the Chief Presidency Magistrate. These petitions were dismissed by the Madras High Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court after the Madras High Court dismissed his criminal revision petitions. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals.

issue.issue_text: Whether s. 297(2) of the 1961 Act is completely exhaustive, or if the provisions of s. 6(e) of the General Clauses Act apply to matters not expressly saved by it.

facts: The appellant was being prosecuted under s. 52 of the Income Tax Act, 1922, for offences related to assessment proceedings that were pending when the 1922 Act was repealed by the Income Tax Act, 1961.
The appellant argued that the prosecution was invalid because the saving clause in the new Act, s. 297(2), did not explicitly provide for the continuation of such prosecutions.
law: Section 6 of the General Clauses Act provides that when an enactment is repealed, any legal proceeding pending under the repealed act can be continued as if the repealing act had not been passed.
This principle applies unless a "different intention" appears in the new, repealing statute.
The question is not whether the new act expressly keeps old rights alive, but whether it manifests an intention to destroy them. The mere absence of a saving clause is not, by itself, material.
application: The Court determined that s. 6 of the General Clauses Act would apply unless the new 1961 Act showed an intention incompatible with or contrary to it.

Upon examining s. 297(2) of the 1961 Act, the Court found no such contrary intention. It concluded that Parliament did not intend to take away the right to institute prosecutions for proceedings that were pending when the new Act commenced.
The Court noted that while s. 297(2) saved certain specific matters, it had not made any detailed provision for the institution of prosecutions for pending proceedings.

The Court clarified a previous ruling, stating that s. 6 of the General Clauses Act is only displaced for matters where the new Act has made detailed, contrary provisions. Since no such provision existed for this situation, s. 6 was not displaced.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that s. 297(2) of the 1961 Act was not completely exhaustive. For matters not expressly saved by it, such as the continuation of prosecutions for pending proceedings, the provisions of s. 6 of the General Clauses Act apply. Therefore, the prosecution of the appellant under the repealed 1922 Act was legally valid.

issue.issue_text: Whether there is any repugnancy or inconsistency between the two relevant enactments, preventing them from standing together.

facts: The appellant argued that there were several differences between Section 177 of the Indian Penal Code and Section 52 of the 1922 Act, which made them inconsistent.

These differences included variations in procedure (e.g., one being non-compoundable), the nature of the punishment, and the fact that the 1922 Act barred prosecution if a penalty was levied, a provision absent in the Indian Penal Code.
law: The court considered the doctrine of implied repeal, which states that a later enactment can repeal an earlier one if they are so inconsistent they cannot coexist.
It also referenced the principle that a new statute providing a new procedure for an existing offence is often considered cumulative, not a replacement, unless it expressly repeals the prior law.
The court cited Section 26 of the General Clauses Act, which allows for prosecution under multiple enactments for the same act but prohibits being punished twice for the same offence.
application: The court determined that the differences between the two laws did not amount to repugnancy or inconsistency.
It reasoned that Section 52 of the 1922 Act did not alter the fundamental nature or quality of the offence described in Section 177 of the Indian Penal Code.
Instead, the 1922 Act merely provided a new, alternative course of procedure for an act that was already an offence.
Citing precedent, the court held that when the legislature does not expressly abolish a prior law, it is presumed to intend for the two remedies to coexist.
Therefore, the court viewed the 1922 Act not as superseding or repealing the prior law, but as being cumulative.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that there was no repugnancy or inconsistency between the two enactments. It held that the statutes could stand together and were cumulative in effect, meaning an offender could be prosecuted under both, though not punished twice for the same offence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the doctrine of implied repeal applies in the circumstances of the case.

facts: The appellant was prosecuted under Section 177 of the Indian Penal Code (a general provision) for offenses related to tax returns.
The appellant argued that this prosecution was illegal because Section 52 of the 1922 Income Tax Act was a special provision covering the same matter.

The appellant contended that the specific provisions of the 1922 Act should be considered to have repealed the general provisions of the Indian Penal Code by implication, pointing to several differences between the two statutes.
law: The court established the legal test for an implied repeal: it can only be concluded if the two enactments are so inconsistent or repugnant that they cannot stand together.
The repeal of the earlier law must be a necessary implication from the language of the later enactment.

When a new statute provides a new procedure or remedy for what is already an offense under a previous law, the new statute is presumed to be cumulative, not a replacement, unless it expressly abolishes the old law.
application: The Court scrutinized the terms of both Section 177 of the Indian Penal Code and Section 52 of the 1922 Act.
It found that the differences between the two statutes did not amount to repugnancy or inconsistency.
The Court reasoned that Section 52 of the 1922 Act did not alter the fundamental nature or quality of the offense already defined in Section 177 of the Indian Penal Code.
Instead, the Court viewed Section 52 as merely providing a "new course of procedure" for an existing offense.
Therefore, the Court determined that the new law was not intended to supersede or repeal the previous law, but rather to be cumulative, meaning both remedies could co-exist.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that there was no repugnancy or inconsistency between the two enactments, and they could stand together. The provisions were treated as cumulative in effect. Consequently, the doctrine of implied repeal was not applicable, and the appellant's argument was rejected.

arguments.issue_text: Whether s. 297(2) of the 1961 Act is completely exhaustive, or if the provisions of s. 6(e) of the General Clauses Act apply to matters not expressly saved by it.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument, as inferred from the court's reasoning, is that since there is no express sub-clause in s. 297(2) of the 1961 Act that saves the continuation of prosecution proceedings started under the 1922 Act, those proceedings are no longer valid.
respondent_arguments: Section 297(2) of the 1961 Act was not intended by Parliament to be completely exhaustive.
For matters not expressly saved by s. 297(2), the provisions of s. 6(e) of the General Clauses Act apply.
Since there is no contrary intention expressed in the 1961 Act, s. 6 of the General Clauses Act is applicable, and the prosecution under the 1922 Act is valid.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there is any repugnancy or inconsistency between the two relevant enactments, preventing them from standing together.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument, as inferred from the court's rejection, is that there is a repugnancy or inconsistency between the two enactments under which they were charged (s. 52 of the 1922 Act and s. 177 of the Indian Penal Code), and therefore they cannot stand together.
respondent_arguments: There is no repugnancy or inconsistency between the two enactments.
The two enactments can stand together and should be treated as cumulative in effect.

As per s. 26 of the General Clauses Act, an act constituting an offense under two enactments allows the offender to be prosecuted under either or both, with the only bar being against being punished twice for the same offense.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the doctrine of implied repeal applies in the circumstances of the case.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the doctrine of implied repeal applies, meaning the later 1961 Act implicitly repealed the relevant provisions of the earlier 1922 Act, thus invalidating the prosecution.
respondent_arguments: The doctrine of implied repeal cannot be applied because there is no repugnancy or inconsistency between the two enactments, and they can be treated as cumulative.

cases.principle: Relied on to explain and interpret the ratio in Kalawati Devi, clarifying that Section 6 of the General Clauses Act will not apply only in respect of those matters where Parliament had clearly expressed its intention to the contrary by making detailed provisions for similar matters.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When an act or omission constitutes an offense under two separate enactments, the offender may be prosecuted and convicted under either or both, but cannot be punished twice for the same offense. A new statute that provides a new procedure for an existing offense is considered cumulative and does not implicitly repeal the previous law, provided there is no repugnancy or inconsistency. Furthermore, when a statute is repealed and re-enacted, legal proceedings under the old act are preserved by Section 6 of the General Clauses Act unless the new legislation manifests a clear intention to destroy them; the mere absence of a specific saving clause for such proceedings is not, by itself, sufficient to establish such a contrary intention.
obiter: The point should be left open and the appellant may urge the argument before the trying magistrate at the time of the commencement of the trial.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the repeal of the 1922 Income-tax Act by the 1961 Act did not invalidate ongoing prosecutions for offenses committed under the old Act. This is because s. 297(2) of the 1961 Act was not intended by Parliament to be completely exhaustive, and in the absence of a contrary intention in the new Act, s. 6 of the General Clauses Act applies to save the pre-existing liability. Furthermore, there is no repugnancy between the relevant penal provisions of the two enactments that would justify an implied repeal, as they can stand together and be treated as cumulative.
legal_tests_applied: The test for the application of s. 6 of the General Clauses Act upon a repeal and re-enactment: 'The question is not whether the new Act expressly keeps alive old rights and liabilities but whether it manifests an intention to destroy them. Section 6 of the General Clauses Act therefore will be applicable uriless the new legislation manifests an intention incompatible with or contrary to the provisions of the section.'

The rule from s. 26 of the General Clauses Act for offenses under two enactments: 'where ll1i act or omission constitutes an offence under two enact-ments, the offender may be prosecuted and punished under either or both ihe enactments but shall not be liable to be punished twice for the same offence.'

The test for implied repeal: The doctrine applies only where there is repugnancy or inconsistency between two enactments; if they can stand together and be treated as cumulative, there is no implied repeal.
why_appellant_lost: The court determined that Parliament did not intend s. 297(2) of the 1961 Act to be completely exhaustive, and the mere absence of an express saving clause for prosecutions was not material enough to indicate an intention to destroy existing liabilities.
The court found 'no repugnancy or inconsistency' between the two enactments, concluding that 'the two enactments can stand together and they must therefore be treated as cumulative in effect.'
Because there was no repugnancy or inconsistency found between the two laws, the court held that 'the doctrine of implied repeal cannot be applied in the circumstances of this case.'
why_respondent_won: The court held that because s. 297(2) of the 1961 Act was not exhaustive and no contrary intention was manifested in the new statute, 'the provisions of s. 6 (e) of the General Clauses Act will apply' to save the prosecution proceedings.
The court found that the two enactments under which the appellant was charged were not inconsistent and could be treated as cumulative, thereby allowing prosecution under either.

The court applied s. 26 of the General Clauses Act, which explicitly permits trial and conviction under two different enactments for the same offense, with the only prohibition being against double punishment.
policy_considerations: The only policy consideration mentioned is the statutory protection against double jeopardy, as articulated in s. 26 of the General Clauses Act, which bars an offender from being 'punished twice for the same offence.'
